title: Astronomers studied winds on 7 distant planets. What they found could change the search for alien life
excerpt: Scientists studying seven extremely hot planets outside our solar system discovered an unusual pattern in their atmospheric winds. The hotter the planets were, the slower their winds appeared to move, suggesting that invisible magnetic fields could be responsible.
content:
Although high wind speeds can cause problems in hot weather here on Earth, can you imagine if a planet had winds that blew faster than 25,000 km/h? The temperatures would be so high that the planet’s atmosphere would function very differently to that of our own planet.

Scientists researching seven such planets have been surprised by their discoveries. Winds seemed to blow more slowly at higher temperatures.

As a rule, warmer temperatures should mean greater energy is available to fuel winds. Therefore, why was this not the case?


A study, published in Nature Astronomy on June 2 2026, indicates that undetectable magnetic fields may be causing the reduction in wind speed. This could offer a fresh method of investigating exoplanets: planets that lie outside our solar system.

So why were scientists investigating wind speeds on seven exoplanets?

Initially, scientists sought to establish whether wind patterns on hot planets are similar.

They analysed seven ‘ultra-hot Jupiter’ planets. These are massive gaseous planets which revolve very quickly around their parent star. Unlike Earth which alternates between day and night as it spins, these planets always present the same face to their star.

One hemisphere is continually exposed to sunlight, whereas the other is perpetually in shadow.

Such vast temperature variations lead to strong winds. Scientists, headed by Julia Seidel of the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur in France, aimed to investigate the nature of these winds.

Yet further discoveries were made.

What did scientists discover about the elusive winds?

Wind speeds were recorded as low as around 7,200 km/h and as high as over 25,000 km/h. While the swiftest winds on Jupiter can attain speeds of around 1,500 km/h, these speeds are much greater.

It was not wind speed which particularly captured the interest of the scientists. They realised that, generally, the hottest planets also had the lowest wind speeds.

This was unexpected. Greater temperatures should typically equate to greater sources of energy to power winds. However, it seemed that another factor was affecting the gas flow.

The scientists thought that magnetic fields may be responsible for this.

So how can magnetic fields reduce the wind speeds of exoplanets?

Although intangible, magnetic fields can be detected.

Our own planet possesses a magnetic field which in turn defends us from potentially harmful streams of charged particles from space. Both Jupiter and Saturn also have magnetic fields.

On ultra-hot planets, temperatures can be so intense that some atoms lose their electrons and become charged. As these charged particles travel through a magnetic field, electromagnetic forces can impede their progress. This is often referred to as magnetic drag.

Scientists think a comparable mechanism could be at work on the seven exoplanets.

The magnetic fields may therefore function as a type of ‘brake’, and so inhibit wind speeds from increasing as much as they otherwise would based purely on temperature variations.

How were wind speeds analysed on planets so far away?

The scientists analysed data collected by the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope in Chile and the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii.

As the exoplanets passed in front of their parent stars, the scientists analysed light that was travelling through the planets’ atmospheres.

By assessing slight variations in the wavelengths of light absorbed by iron atoms, they were able to approximate the speed of gas within the atmospheres.

This is based on the so-called Doppler effect.

Scientists then cross-referenced this data with atmospheric modelling in order to assess the likely strength of the exoplanets’ magnetic fields. Their results indicated that the magnetic fields could be as strong as a few gauss – similar to those on planets in our solar system.

Again, however, these were not directly observed, but were deduced from analysing wind speeds.

Could this research aid the search for aliens?

Whilst the seven planets are not thought to possess environments appropriate for known forms of life (due to excessively high temperatures), the research may still prove valuable in this area.

Magnetic fields can affect how a planet responds to radiation and charged particles from its parent star. In certain situations, they may even assist in shielding a planet’s atmosphere from being eroded.

Eventually, an improved understanding of magnetic fields may therefore allow scientists to investigate smaller planets which could potentially support life.

Looking ahead, scientists hope to gather further data using the Extremely Large Telescope.

In the meantime, this research highlights an intriguing option.

Whilst it may not be possible to directly observe the magnetic field of a distant planet, scientists may be able to analyse atmospheric dynamics in order to determine if such a field exists.
